references.text: When Lazarus was raised from the dead, many Jews believed in Jesus, but not all. This illustrates exactly the point of Abraham's reply: even someone who comes back from the dead will not convince those who refuse to believe ([ref:Joh 11:43-44|John 11:43-44]).

After Lazarus was raised from the dead, the chief priests planned to kill him instead of repenting – a direct fulfillment of the point in the parable that even a resurrection will not lead to repentance among the hardened-hearted ([ref:Joh 12:10-11|John 12:10-11]).

Abraham's reply in the next verse is the decisive answer to the rich man's plea: If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead ([ref:Luk 16:31|Luke 16:31]).

Paul preached about the resurrection in Athens, but many mocked and refused to believe, showing that even testimony of a resurrection from the dead does not automatically lead to repentance ([ref:Apg 17:30-32|Acts 17:30-32]).
Paul testified about Christ's resurrection before King Agrippa, but Agrippa was not convinced to repent, despite the testimony of one who had risen from the dead ([ref:Apg 26:22-23|Acts 26:22-23]).

Jesus says that whoever does not believe Moses' writings will not believe his words either – the same principle Abraham expresses here: God's revealed word in Scripture is sufficient, and miracles do not convince those who reject Scripture ([ref:Joh 5:45-47|John 5:45-47]).

Jesus rejects the demand for a sign and points to the sign of Jonah. The men of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, but this generation seeks extraordinary signs instead of listening to God's word ([ref:Luk 11:29-32|Luke 11:29-32]).

Abraham had already interceded for Sodom, but righteousness and judgment stood firm. The rich man's appeal to "father Abraham" to send someone from the dead reflects a tradition of appealing to Abraham as an intercessor ([ref:1 Mos 18:23-25|Genesis 18:23-25]).
